Deployment · 2026-11-13

Finding the useful throughput frontier

A faster batch is useful only while every user still gets an acceptable stream. We measured Kimi-K3 on eleven hardware configurations and drew the line at 40 tok/s per user.

1,991tok/s total, 41 tok/s per user, 2×B200
496tok/s at the line, recommended 2×H200
34/34official interface tests passed

On this page

The questionThe layouts we ranThroughput at the lineWhat the numbers taught usThe cost lineData & sources

The question

Adding concurrency always raises total throughput for a while. But every user sees a slower stream. So we only count throughput while each user still gets at least 40 tokens per second, and compare configurations at that point. Workload: about 7.6K input tokens per request with unique prefixes (no cache hits) and 1,024 output tokens; concurrency 1/4/16/32/64, two rounds each.

The layouts we ran

Each box below is one eight-GPU machine with tensor parallelism inside it; arrows are pipeline hand-offs; the strip shows how the 93 layers are split.

Throughput at the line

Fastest: 2×B200 with tensor parallelism inside each machine, two pipeline stages, EFA networking, DSpark speculative decoding with k=2 and fp8 KV. Single request 177 tok/s with a 0.38 s first token. At 64 concurrent requests each user still gets 41 tok/s and the total is 1,991 tok/s, or 124 per GPU, 4.0× the 2×H200 layout. Peak reached 2,348 tok/s at 96 concurrency (about 34 per user). Correctness checks passed (OCRBench 0.890, MMMU Pro 0.799, tool schema 408/408); full acceptance is still pending.

Recommended today: 2×H200 with k=4. At 16 concurrency each user gets 40 tok/s and the total is 496 tok/s (31 per GPU), the highest per-GPU number among full-model layouts at the line. It passed all 34 official interface tests, 18 cross-model tests and our team acceptance. To scale, add replicas rather than pipeline stages.

What the numbers taught us

  • Speculative decoding is mandatory. Without it, 63 tok/s; with DSpark, 125 tok/s. On H200, k=4 keeps single-request speed and gives 17% more throughput at 16 concurrency than k=8.
  • Throughput peaks around 32 concurrency on 2×H200 (645 tok/s) and falls at 64 (579 tok/s, 20 tok/s per user, 21 s first token). The KV pool is the ceiling.
  • Pruning hurts the long tail. A community build that removes half the experts (REAP-448) is fast and passes the interface tests, but in scenes that should call a question tool it answered in text about 40% of the time (21 calls out of 36).
  • Measure throughput honestly. Throughput is total output tokens divided by wall-clock time. Earlier internal reports summed per-request speeds and overstated throughput by 2.3–2.5×; every number here was recomputed from raw per-request data.

The cost line

On this workload, 2×B200 costs about $17 per million output tokens, under the roughly $31 market median, so even short chats are profitable. 2×H200 costs $39 and only breaks even at about $3.47 per GPU-hour. Agent traffic with high cache hit rates changes the economics in our favor; that is the traffic we design for.
